title: Behavioral-health improvement among younger Americans coexists with a large and uneven adult burden
source_unit: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Key Substance Use and Mental Health Indicators in the United States: Results from the 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, July 2026
geography: United States; civilian, noninstitutionalized population aged 12 or older

observations.period: 2021-2025; behavioral-health indicators among adolescents and young adults

youth_direction.value: SAMHSA reports that adolescents ages 12 to 17 and young adults ages 18 to 25 continued to show downward or stable trends in most behavioral-health indicators over the five-year series

adolescent_illicit_drug_use.value: past-year illicit-drug use among adolescents declined from 14.6% in 2021 to 11.2% in 2025

adolescent_drug_use_disorder.value: past-year drug-use disorder among adolescents declined from 7.3% in 2021 to 5.9% in 2025

young_adult_sud.value: past-year substance-use disorder among young adults declined from 26.2% in 2021 to 23.8% in 2025
young_adult_sud.unit: percent of young adults ages 18 to 25

observations.method: Annual NSDUH estimates and 2021-2025 trend comparisons for substance use, substance-use disorder, mental illness, suicidality, and treatment.
observations.uncertainty: The report describes population-level associations and trend differences; it does not establish which policies, social conditions, products, or behaviors caused the changes.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents ages 12 to 17 and young adults ages 18 to 25.
observations.counterinterpretation: A downward survey trend does not mean that behavioral-health risk is low or evenly distributed; definitions, reporting, access to care, and subgroup composition can affect the observed pattern.

denominator.unit: adults aged 18 or older in the 2025 NSDUH

any_mental_illness.unit: percent of adults with any mental illness in the past year; 54.6 million people

serious_mental_illness.unit: percent of adults with serious mental illness in the past year; 18.2 million people

young_adult_combined_burden.unit: percent of young adults ages 18 to 25 with any mental illness or substance-use disorder in the past year; 14.9 million people

adult_system_scale.value: behavioral health remains a large population-scale care, work, household, and public-system issue even as selected youth indicators improve

observations.method: Nationally representative annual survey of the U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized population aged 12 or older.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are survey-based and do not by themselves describe severity, duration, functional impairment, treatment quality, or outcomes for every person counted.
observations.subgroup: Adults overall, with an especially high combined mental-illness or substance-use-disorder share among young adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher reported prevalence can reflect improved recognition or disclosure as well as need; prevalence is not equivalent to a clinical treatment requirement or an inevitable loss of work capacity.

observations.period: 2025; mental-health treatment among adults with serious mental illness

denominator.unit: adults aged 18 or older with serious mental illness in the past year

young_adult_treatment.unit: percent of adults ages 18 to 25 with serious mental illness who received mental-health treatment in the past year; 2.8 million people

midlife_treatment.unit: percent of adults ages 26 to 49 with serious mental illness who received mental-health treatment in the past year; 6.9 million people

older_adult_treatment.unit: percent of adults ages 50 or older with serious mental illness who received mental-health treatment in the past year; 2.6 million people

access_gradient.value: treatment receipt was lower among young adults than among older adult age groups

observations.method: NSDUH self-reports of past-year serious mental illness and mental-health treatment, with age-group comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: Treatment receipt does not measure timeliness, affordability, continuity, adequacy, patient choice, or clinical benefit; the age comparison does not identify the mechanism of the gap.
observations.subgroup: Adults with past-year serious mental illness, especially young adults ages 18 to 25.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age differences may reflect need, insurance, eligibility, stigma, provider supply, treatment preference, family support, or measurement differences rather than a single access failure.

denominator.unit: people aged 12 or older in the United States

any_major_substance_past_month.unit: percent who used tobacco, vaped nicotine, used alcohol, or used an illicit drug in the past month; 162.8 million people

alcohol_past_month.unit: percent who drank alcohol in the past month; 129.1 million people

marijuana_past_year.unit: percent who used marijuana in the past year; 61.6 million people

market_and_routine_reach.value: substance use remains a mass everyday-behavior and consumer-environment issue, not only a small clinical subgroup issue

observations.method: NSDUH national estimates of past-month and past-year substance use across age groups.
observations.uncertainty: The measures do not distinguish moderate use, risky use, dependence, legal status, product intensity, or downstream health and spending effects for every user.
observations.subgroup: People ages 12 or older, with separate estimates reported for adolescents, young adults, and older adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad reach does not imply uniform harm or a single cultural meaning; the same category includes different products, frequencies, contexts, and levels of risk.

related_sources.claim: SAMHSA's detailed tables provide the underlying national estimates and age-specific comparisons for substance use, mental health, and treatment.

boundary: This record adds a behavioral-health transition pattern: several adolescent and young-adult indicators improved or held steady from 2021 to 2025, while adult mental-health burden remains large, treatment receipt varies by age, and substance use reaches a broad population. It does not establish causes, individual clinical need, treatment quality, or subgroup-level mechanisms beyond the published comparisons.
